learning_goal: Say what a disc joins, why it is thickest in the lumbar region, and why a prolapse goes backwards and to the side rather than forwards.

structures.name: intervertebral disk of fourth lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L4/5 disc — the exemplar
structures.narration: The pad between the bodies of L4 and L5. It is a joint, not a spacer: a secondary cartilaginous joint that allows a little movement at every level and a lot over the whole column.

structures.name: intervertebral disk of fifth lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L5/S1 disc — the lumbosacral disc
structures.narration: The lowest and the most wedged disc, sitting on the sloping top of the sacrum. It carries the most load and is one of the two levels that prolapse most often.

structures.name: intervertebral disk of sixth thoracic vertebra
structures.label: T6/7 disc — thoracic
structures.narration: Thin relative to its vertebral body, and splinted by the ribs. Little movement is asked of it, and thoracic discs rarely prolapse.

structures.name: intervertebral disk of fifth cervical vertebra
structures.label: C5/6 disc — cervical
structures.narration: Small, but thick for the size of its body — which is why the neck is the most mobile region despite having the smallest bones.

structures.name: intervertebral disk of first lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L1/2 disc
structures.narration: One of the stack — every level has the same construction.

structures.name: intervertebral disk of second lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L2/3 disc

structures.name: intervertebral disk of third lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L3/4 disc

structures.name: second lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L2
structures.narration: A lumbar body — one half of the joint above and below it.

structures.name: fourth lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L4 — above the exemplar
structures.narration: The vertebra above the exemplar disc. Its lower surface is one face of the joint.

structures.name: fifth lumbar vertebra
structures.label: L5 — below the exemplar
structures.narration: The vertebra below. Its upper surface is the other face — the disc is glued to both.

structures.name: sacrum
structures.label: Sacrum
structures.narration: The sloping platform the last disc sits on.

structures.name: sixth thoracic vertebra
structures.label: T6
structures.narration: Thoracic body, for scale against its disc.

structures.name: fifth cervical vertebra
structures.label: C5
structures.narration: Cervical body, for scale against its disc.

views.title: Where the discs sit
views.narration: A disc lies between the bodies of every two neighbouring vertebrae, from the axis down to the sacrum. Twenty-three in all — there is no disc between the atlas and the axis. Together they make up about a quarter of the column's height.

views.title: One joint, two bones
views.narration: Strip away the rest and the joint is simple: two vertebral bodies with one pad between them, bound to the end plate of each. Bone, cartilage, bone — a symphysis, which is why it moves a little and never dislocates.

views.title: Soft centre, tough ring
views.narration: Cut across it. The outer part is the annulus fibrosus — concentric rings of fibrocartilage running in alternating directions, thick in front and thinner behind. At the centre sits the nucleus pulposus, a gel that is largely water. The nucleus takes the pressure and the annulus holds it in; when the annulus tears, the nucleus is what escapes.

views.title: Why a prolapse goes backwards and sideways
views.narration: Load runs down the bodies and through every disc, heaviest at the bottom. Bending forward squeezes the front of the disc and drives the nucleus backwards. The annulus is thinnest behind, and the posterior longitudinal ligament reinforces the middle of the back wall — so the weak point is behind and to the side. That is where the nucleus escapes, and that is where the nerve root is.

views.title: The nerve next door
views.narration: The gap between two pedicles is the intervertebral foramen, and it lies just behind and above the disc. The nerve leaving there is the one named for the vertebra above — but a posterolateral prolapse at L4/5 usually misses that nerve and catches the one crossing to the level below, giving L5 symptoms. L5/S1 catches S1. Learn the pair: the level of the disc and the root it traps are not the same number.

views.title: Thicker where you bend
views.narration: Disc thickness tracks movement, not size. The cervical discs are thick for their small bodies and the neck is mobile. The thoracic discs are thin and the ribs hold that region still. The lumbar discs are the thickest of all, and the loin bends most — and pays for it.

views.title: Take the discs away
views.narration: Remove them and the bodies sit bone on bone. Every millimetre of bending in the column is borrowed from these pads, and the height you lose during the day — and with age — is water leaving them.

gaps: Nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus have no separate entries in the catalog — the smallest unit it holds is the whole disc. The cross-section beat therefore teaches the two zones by narration over a solid disc rather than by two labelled parts. Two models, or one measured anchor at the centre of the nucleus, would make that beat literal.

No spinal nerve, nerve root or cauda equina exists in the catalog (the only nerves it holds are the two optic nerves), so the root a prolapse traps is described but never shown. The 'nerve next door' beat is deliberately authored anyway: the day a nerve model exists it becomes a SHOW_RELATIONSHIP with no other edit.
The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments are absent from the catalog, so the reason the back wall fails posterolaterally rather than in the midline is narrated, not seen.
Vertebral end plates are not separate models either; the disc-to-bone attachment is shown as contact between meshes.
